title: Human regulatory elements without mammalian conservation show a rare-variant excess of only 2-7% of that at conserved DNA once controls match mappability and transposon type (76,215 genomes)
abstract: ENCODE candidate regulatory elements (cCREs) that contain no base conserved across 241 mammals carry only a very small excess of rare variants in 76,215 human genomes: about 2% of the excess at conserved non-coding DNA (sampling upper limit 4%; with the bias seen in negative-control flanks, up to about 7%). This matters because a well-known claim says that biochemically active but non-conserved DNA is under human-specific selection and adds about 4% of the genome to the functional fraction. Purifying selection keeps harmful alleles rare, so it increases the fraction of singletons (variants seen once). We measured this singleton excess for non-CpG single-nucleotide variants from gnomAD v4.1 in 2.12 million autosomal cCREs against matched variants outside cCREs, and divided it by the excess at non-coding bases conserved across mammals (Zoonomia phyloP >= 2.27): the conserved-equivalent fraction. With all sites and simple controls, the 519,501 cCREs with no conserved base (122 Mb) gave 14%, close to the 11.5% reported in 2013. Two technical factors explained most of this. Restriction to fully mappable sites (413 million variants) reduced it to 0.5-4.9%, and controls from transposon copies of the same class and age in the same 1-Mb block reduced it to 1.5-1.9% (95% interval 0.1-3.7%; rare alleles -0.3% to 1.7%; African-ancestry genomes about 0%). A depletion test calibrated by the Roulette per-site mutation-rate model (chromosomes 20-22) was consistent with this: these cCREs had the expected number of variants (observed/expected 0.9995, 95% interval 0.994-1.006), while conserved bases had 6.5% fewer. The largest residual signal was in young transposon copies (about 10% of these variants; 9-21% depending on the statistic), where mapping problems remain possible. Non-conserved bases inside partly conserved cCREs kept a small signal (9-15%). All non-conserved cCRE bases together correspond to about 35-37 Mb of conserved-equivalent sequence (about 50-55 Mb after correction for the lower mutation rate of conserved bases), against 129 Mb reported in 2013. Conserved bases mutate more slowly (rate matching removed 31% of their excess), and CpG sites in cCREs show large false excesses. The main limitation is systematic error: negative-control flanks deviate by up to about 7% of the reference effect, more than the sampling error; the primary controls were chosen after an independent review. Code and a conservation tier for every autosomal cCRE are included.

display.caption: Conserved-equivalent fraction of the human singleton excess (non-CpG SNVs at fully mappable sites, gnomAD v4.1) for ENCODE cCREs by conservation tier and class. Tier 0 = no base with Zoonomia phyloP >= 2.27. Blue: controls from the same 1-Mb block (mutation class, GC, transposon yes/no). Orange: same block, also matched for transposon class and age. Green: transposon subfamily, per-base phyloP and region covariates. 95% block-bootstrap intervals. Dashed line: the 11.5% estimate of Ward & Kellis 2013.

Mutation-rate calibration on chromosomes 20-22. Left: observed / expected gnomAD SNVs at all possible non-CpG substitutions, expected from the Roulette mutation-rate model and matched non-cCRE controls; conserved bases are depleted by about 6.5%, tier-0 cCREs not at all. Right: singleton excess with and without Roulette-rate matching; matching reduces the reference excess at conserved bases, and motif cores (mainly CTCF) show deficits that selection cannot explain.

Singleton excess against controls from the same 1-Mb block, by Zoonomia phyloP of the base, inside and outside cCREs (fully mappable non-CpG sites), for all genomes and for African-ancestry genomes. The excess follows conservation in the same way inside and outside cCREs; its slope inside the non-conserved range shows that per-base phyloP also tracks properties other than selection.
